articles.title: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
articles.summary: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.
articles.content:
After more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

The finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

At the center of the discovery is a particle called B d , which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for new particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

One reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

By measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

The decay known as B d → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called B s . In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of B s → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer B d decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for B d → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The B s decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the B d process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

Following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

"Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," said Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background."

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a new phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

Using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of B d → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related B s → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Although the new findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, B d → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

The High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up new possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles."

For physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the new evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.

The article provides detailed context about the experiment, its significance, and future prospects, fulfilling the criteria for good news.

The team combined new data with older results to reach a high level of confidence.

These improvements will allow researchers to collect even more data and observe more rare decays. That will help confirm this discovery fully and possibly reveal new particles or forces.

articles.title: PhDs worldwide are having a shake up — why now?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03017-yGovernment-supported initiatives around the globe aim to change the PhD, with the goal of providing fresh talent to the private sector.
articles.content:
Industrial PhD programmes are increasingly being utilized in fields such as public engineering.Credit: Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty

Yifan Wang didn’t realize that his thesis would be the first of its kind when he started his PhD, although he knew it was likely to be more applied than most. By the beginning of his project in electrical engineering and telecommunications at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, Wang had already established a connection with an industry partner to gather insights from network traffic patterns — such as how users stream videos.

But after Wang began his research, Australia rolled out its National Industry PhD Programme, in which students undertake research projects co-designed by universities and companies in return for a funding boost from the government and industry partners. The goal, according to the programme’s website, is to “create a flexible pipeline of researchers who can transition between academia and industry and have multiple career pathways open to them after completing their PhD”.

Wang joined the programme’s inaugural class in 2023 and spent the remaining three years of his degree not only with an eye towards practical applications, but also with a community of peers spread across Australia. And in May, he became the first student in the programme to submit his thesis.

Cake to the rescue: how these PhD students are cooking up a sense of community

“At the beginning of my PhD, I was a bit hesitant about whether I would want to do an engineering industry job or a research job,” Wang says. “But now, I’ve found my interest. I’m really determined to find a research position that solves real industry problems.”

As of June, the Australian programme has funded 448 awards and has received more than 1,000 applications during seven funding rounds. And it’s just one of many innovative PhD models. Governments in many other countries have launched programmes supporting industry-oriented PhDs.

“There’s certainly a lot of [experimental programmes] occurring around the world,” says Anthony Boccanfuso, chief executive of the University–Industry Demonstration Partnership, a non-profit organization in Columbia, South Carolina. The partnership leads the Industry-Integrated PhD (I-PhD) programme in the United States, which was launched in July. Although Boccanfuso says that conversations about re-evaluating the PhD model have existed for the past 15–20 years, there’s now a “sense of urgency because of this need for talent” in high-demand fields.

Intelligent manufacturing for rail transit systems is one of several areas to have benefited from China’s industrial PhD scheme.Credit: Xiao Benxiang/VCG/Getty

At the same time, researchers worry that the programmes might take away from fundamental research. When the I-PhD programme launched, chemistry Nobel laureate Carolyn Bertozzi wrote on the social-media website Bluesky that “most PhD students pursue industry jobs anyways — that has always been true. Use NSF funds to support basic science that industry won’t support”.

Aligning interests

Boccanfuso’s organization will oversee more than 250 students with funding from the US National Science Foundation — which will make a US$47-million investment over the next five years — along with industry and university partners. Students are jointly mentored by university and industry advisers and are expected to spend at least one year completing on-site industry research. The programme aims to reduce the time taken to complete a PhD in the United States, from an average of 5.6 years to just 4 years. It will also prepare STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) students for industry careers, which is where most of them are going, Boccanfuso says. Although the initiative is only just beginning, it’s already received “overwhelming interest” from students and universities, he adds. Elsewhere in the world, including in China and the European Union, similar programmes have taken off.

As for why there’s been such a boom in these national-level initiatives, “it’s pretty straightforward”, says João Pereira, a civil engineer at the University of Minho in Guimarães, Portugal, who manages one EU-funded initiative. “It’s much easier to justify applied research than fundamental research because of the proximity to yielding results.” It can take decades for fundamental research to come to fruition, whereas applied research can deliver commercial applications — and therefore money and economic growth — “not immediately, but pretty close to it”, he adds.

Joshua Twiggs, who works in the medical technology industry in Sydney, Australia, and has supervised industry PhDs, says that these initiatives aim to harness a country’s already sophisticated education system as a driver of innovation. “How do we leverage the incredibly smart work happening in universities through to actual industry implementations?” Twiggs says.

Such programmes reflect “the growing recognition that knowledge is a key driver of economic competitiveness and innovation”, says Hans Parmar, a spokesperson from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada in Ottawa, a government department focused on industry, commerce and scientific research. “Modern innovations are often too complex for a single individual, organization or even sector to develop alone,” Parmar adds. But these spanning initiatives mean that governments, universities and industries can all align their interests.

Julie Dubuit is a civil engineer at the University of Toulouse who took part in France’s Industrial Agreements for Training through Research PhD programme.Credit: Julie Dubuit

The trend can also be assigned to “the fact that academic positions in universities can only absorb a small fraction of PhD graduates”, says an official at the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch. That makes “industrial PhDs very attractive with regards to future employment”.

Around the world

Meanwhile, China awarded its first batch of ‘practical PhDs’ in September last year. Rather than completing a conventional thesis, these students develop an innovative product, project or technique — such as intelligent manufacturing in rail transit systems. Since the law allowing these PhDs came into effect last year, more than 60 researchers have received practical PhDs.

“We encourage students to implement ideas that can meet real demand in society, rather than just coming up with concepts,” says Liu Chun, executive dean of the National College of Elite Engineers at Tongji University in Shanghai. Candidates’ success could be measured by “how many patents a student has, how many international or domestic industry standards they have participated in setting and whether their product has successfully passed a pilot test”, Chun says.

NSF rolls out ‘industry PhD’ programme — joining a global trend

The European Union’s Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) programme offers applicants the opportunity to be part of industrial-doctorate networks of students, all of whom are focused on a single research topic. Each student has both an academic and a non-academic supervisor and must spend at least half of their fellowship on the premises of the non-academic partner. When all the cohort members and their supervisors come together, “it’s almost like a small conference”, says Pereira, who is part of a network that explores sustainable construction. “All these interactions force students to create a set of skills they won’t get anywhere else.”

One of the programme’s main goals, according to the European Commission official, is to “nourish the talent pipeline for boosting employability in industry”. A 2025 study found that two years after completing their fellowships, 66% of industrial doctorate graduates were working outside academia, compared with just 43% of graduates from the MSCA’s standard doctoral networks1.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a global shift in PhD education towards industry-integrated programs that provide practical skills and improve employability, benefiting students, industries, and economies. This represents a significant, positive change in higher education with broad societal impact, supported by government initiatives and detailed examples from multiple countries.
articles.personality_title: New PhD programs connect students with industry to boost careers and innovation
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – PhD degrees traditionally focus on deep academic research, but many graduates find jobs in industries like technology or engineering. Governments worldwide are now creating programs that link PhD students directly with companies to make their research more practical and improve job opportunities.

**What happened** – In 2023, Australia launched the National Industry PhD Programme, where students work on projects designed with both universities and businesses. Yifan Wang was the first to finish his thesis under this program, which helps students gain real-world experience while studying. Similar programs have started in the US, China, the EU, and Canada, supported by government funding and partnerships.

**Impact** – These new PhD models aim to shorten the time it takes to get a degree and prepare students for jobs outside universities. For example, the US program hopes to reduce PhD completion from about 5.6 years to 4 years. Students get mentorship from both academic and industry experts and spend time working at companies. This approach helps students develop skills that traditional PhDs may not teach, making them ready for careers in fast-changing fields like engineering or medical technology.

**What's next step** – Governments and universities will continue expanding these programs and tracking their success. As more students graduate with industry-focused PhDs, companies may benefit from fresh ideas and innovations. The programs could also inspire changes in how research is done, balancing practical projects with fundamental science.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New government-backed PhD programs worldwide are helping students gain practical experience and quicker paths to careers by partnering universities with industries.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouveaux doctorats relient étudiants et entreprises pour booster carrières et innovation
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les doctorats se concentrent souvent sur la recherche académique, mais de nombreux diplômés travaillent dans l’industrie. Pour mieux préparer ces étudiants, plusieurs gouvernements ont créé des programmes qui associent les doctorants aux entreprises afin de rendre leur recherche plus pratique et d’améliorer leurs chances d’emploi.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2023, l’Australie a lancé le Programme national de doctorat industriel, où les étudiants réalisent des projets conçus avec des universités et des entreprises. Yifan Wang a été le premier à terminer sa thèse dans ce cadre, qui permet d’acquérir une expérience concrète pendant les études. Des programmes similaires ont démarré aux États-Unis, en Chine, dans l’UE et au Canada, soutenus par des financements publics et des partenariats.

**Impact** – Ces nouveaux modèles de doctorat veulent raccourcir la durée des études et préparer les étudiants à des emplois hors université. Par exemple, le programme américain vise à réduire la durée moyenne d’un doctorat de 5,6 à 4 ans. Les étudiants sont encadrés par des experts académiques et industriels et passent du temps en entreprise. Cette méthode leur permet d’acquérir des compétences souvent absentes des doctorats classiques, utiles dans des domaines en évolution rapide comme l’ingénierie ou la technologie médicale.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les gouvernements et universités vont continuer à développer ces programmes et à en mesurer les résultats. Au fur et à mesure que des étudiants diplômés de doctorats orientés industrie entreront sur le marché, les entreprises pourraient bénéficier d’idées nouvelles et d’innovations. Ces programmes pourraient aussi influencer les pratiques de recherche, en équilibrant projets appliqués et science fondamentale.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De nouveaux programmes doctoraux soutenus par les gouvernements aident les étudiants à acquérir une expérience pratique et un accès plus rapide à l’emploi grâce à des partenariats entre universités et entreprises.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos doctorados conectan estudiantes con empresas para impulsar carreras e innovación
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los doctorados suelen centrarse en la investigación académica profunda, pero muchos graduados trabajan en industrias como tecnología o ingeniería. Por eso, gobiernos de todo el mundo están creando programas que vinculan a estudiantes de doctorado directamente con empresas para hacer su investigación más práctica y mejorar sus oportunidades laborales.

**Qué pasó** – En 2023, Australia lanzó el Programa Nacional de Doctorado Industrial, donde los estudiantes trabajan en proyectos diseñados junto a universidades y empresas. Yifan Wang fue el primero en terminar su tesis bajo este programa, que ayuda a los estudiantes a ganar experiencia real mientras estudian. Programas similares han empezado en Estados Unidos, China, la Unión Europea y Canadá, con apoyo de fondos y asociaciones gubernamentales.

**Impacto** – Estos nuevos modelos de doctorado buscan reducir el tiempo para obtener el título y preparar a los estudiantes para trabajos fuera de la academia. Por ejemplo, el programa estadounidense espera bajar el promedio de 5.6 años a 4 años. Los estudiantes reciben mentoría de expertos académicos y de la industria y pasan tiempo trabajando en empresas. Esto les permite desarrollar habilidades que los doctorados tradicionales no enseñan, preparándolos para carreras en campos que cambian rápido como la ingeniería o tecnología médica.

**Próximo paso** – Los gobiernos y universidades seguirán ampliando estos programas y evaluando sus resultados. A medida que más estudiantes se gradúen con doctorados orientados a la industria, las empresas podrán beneficiarse de ideas nuevas e innovaciones. Estos programas también podrían inspirar cambios en la forma de hacer investigación, equilibrando proyectos prácticos con ciencia básica.

**Resumen en una frase** – Nuevos programas de doctorado apoyados por gobiernos están ayudando a estudiantes a obtener experiencia práctica y caminos más rápidos hacia carreras mediante asociaciones entre universidades e industrias.

articles.title: Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past
articles.summary: A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time
articles.content:
A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time

Ada Zielinska

Today, for breakfast, I had a smoothie. This isn’t unusual: I drink the same smoothie every weekday morning. At some point in the past, I discovered I particularly liked it and made it a habit. It is a simple example of something that makes intuitive sense – that our past experiences determine our present actions, and they, in turn, determine our future trajectories.

But what if I told you that the past never actually existed? Or, at least, that it doesn’t matter? It sounds left field, but I would only be channelling an assumption that lurks within many laws of physics largely unchallenged: that the present moment is all we need to know about to predict the future. Without making this assumption, the amount of information you need to predict the future is at risk of dramatically blowing up, rapidly making it impractical to say anything at all.

Or so we thought. Now, there’s a move afoot to reclaim the past for physics. Its proponents think that could resolve long-standing questions at the core of quantum theory, such as why it is so weird as it is, but equally not as weird as it could be – and, along the way, clarify the true nature of time itself. “I think it’s a big deal. I think it will be a big thing for the foundations of physics,” says quantum information researcher Jacob Biamonte at École de Technologie Supérieure in Montreal.

Advertisement

To begin to understand how physics cancelled the past, imagine a game of marbles. To predict where any marble will be in a second’s time, all we need to know is its current position, speed and direction of travel, all effectively ignorant of the marble’s deep past. We then roll the relevant physical laws – in this case, Isaac Newton’s laws of motion – forward into the future. We don’t need to know anything about the collisions that brought the marble to its present position – luckily, as calculating the myriad past possibilities might rapidly overwhelm our computational ability.

The marble’s present is agnostic about its past, and its past is largely immaterial in determining its future, so long as we know about the present. It is like saying that all that matters with my smoothie choice is that memories of past mornings are stored in my present mind. Even if the past vanished entirely, I can continue my breakfast routine. In this way of thinking, there’s no way of telling if the universe began just 5 minutes ago.

This principle of neglecting the past is called Markovianity, after Andrey Markov, the Russian mathematician who laid the groundwork for the idea. And it is everywhere in physics – even in quantum theory, our best stab at characterising how the weird realm of particles behaves.

Unlike objects in the classical world, quantum particles can appear to be in a mix of different states at once – in multiple positions, for example. This leads to dramas such as the infamous Schrödinger’s cat thought experiment, in which a cat is kept in a box in a quantum “superposition” of being alive and dead. Each of the two states can be assigned its own probability, encoded in a mathematical object called the quantum wave function.

Just as with classical mechanics, standard quantum mechanics doesn’t much care about the cat’s past. As far as its future goes, there are two possibilities. You can keep the box closed, in which case, all you can say is a matter of percentages – the cat could be alive or dead and currently seems to be existentially fuzzy. Or you open the box, in which case, the cat’s wave function “collapses” into a single, definitive state and the animal is definitively dead or alive, too.

Schrödinger’s cat lifted the lid on a load of problems that physicists and philosophers have anguished over in the century since the inception of quantum mechanics. What physically happens when you open the box – is it you who somehow potentially kills the cat? What about the nanosecond when you have just barely moved the lid – is the cat somehow slightly less mixed at this time? What, indeed, does anything about the wave function say about the cat in the real, physical world? Is the wave function itself “real”? “It’s been 100 years, and we still don’t have a consensus on the right way to think about quantum theory,” says philosopher David Glick at the University of California, Davis.

Jacob Barandes, a philosopher of physics at Harvard University, thinks he has identified the problem. He says that the shenanigans surrounding the wave function are merely a smokescreen, behind which the true culprit for the cat’s bizarre situation is hiding: the influence of the past.

What actually happens when Schrödinger’s cat is in the box? Westend61 GmbH/Alamy

In a paper published last year, he showed that something like quantum theory can be built on equations for inherently probabilistic, non-Markovian processes that are always influenced by their past. In this world, cats are never simultaneously dead and alive; rather, everything is inherently chancy, and the past indispensable.

Here, the wave function doesn’t represent any physical reality, but is just a form of mathematical bookkeeping for all the ways in which the past touches the cat from across time. Let’s go back to our marble and make it quantum. Barandes likens this marble’s wave function to a collection of “ghost marbles”. Each of these ghost marbles embodies the real quantum marble’s state but, say, 1 second ago – or 2, or 3, or as far back as you like. “Each ghost marble is a little weird. It’s invisible. It’s unobservable,” says Barandes. But if you have information about the ghost marbles, you can predict what the real marble can do next. Consequently, the world that contains real and ghost marbles seems to follow tractable, Markovian laws, because everything about the real marble’s past is encoded in the ghost marbles’ present. The price of pretending that the past doesn’t matter is filling the universe with ghosts. The quantum wave function is just an elegant arrangement of such spectres.

Barandes thinks our mistake is to read physical reality into this spooky parlour trick. In his alternative framework, quantum peculiarities such as superposition states and wave function collapse are consequences of treating the wave function as something overly real. We can’t know what state Schrödinger’s cat is in, not because its state is somehow existentially fuzzy, but because quantum objects are inherently a little random. “They’re always behaving probabilistically, in a chancy way that depends on the past,” says Barandes. Acts of measurement, such as opening the cat’s box, aren’t special, but merely physical interactions that make the object “forget” some of this past, suppressing some of its chanciness and history-ladenness.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter

This picture provides a way to counter the objection that calculations become intractable if you must account for the whole prior history of the universe. In standard quantum theory, it is well accepted that as objects get larger and interact with more of their environment, they lose their quantumness. In Barandes’s picture, that maps onto objects relinquishing some of their past and becoming more Markovian as the past recedes into the distance.

His framework hasn’t yet produced a distinct, experimentally testable prediction, but it has already had one notable win: explaining the degree to which quantum objects can be correlated, thanks to the phenomenon of quantum entanglement.

When two quantum objects are entangled, the results of measurements of their properties maintain a correlation, even if they are first pulled very far apart. These correlations are stronger than would be possible with any non-quantum connection – by a maximum of about 41 per cent, a number known as the Tsirelson bound. Mathematician Boris Tsirelson derived this number in 1980 from standard quantum theory, but Barandes says it had never been explained beyond being a quirk of complicated mathematics. Later, in 1994, physicists Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich showed that some hypothetical theories could, in principle, achieve correlations 100 per cent greater than non-quantum theories without information being exchanged faster than light speed, which would contradict Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity. “Forty-one per cent is not even half of 100 per cent, so why so little?” asks Barandes.

His framework elegantly brings this back to the speed of light. In a universe of quantum marbles, each marble moves in its slightly random and history-laden way, but because it can’t move or communicate with other marbles faster than light, those parts of its past that lie beyond a horizon of influence set by the speed of light can be neglected. Working with David Kagan and Mahmudul Hasan at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, Barandes has calculated that this constraint is exactly what keeps the strength of quantum correlations from exceeding the Tsirelson bound.

Simon Milz, a physicist at Heriot-Watt University in the UK, is intrigued. Standard quantum theory is very abstract and mysterious, so there is value in uncovering processes that offer some underlying picture, he says – and the Tsirelson bound is one of the most talked-about things in quantum information theory. “It’s quite an interesting thing to find a new principle that leads to it,” says Milz.

David Wallace, a philosopher of physics at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania, echoes that. But he is uncertain how far Barandes’s approach can go, in particular because of the way it denies the wave function any physical reality. Standard quantum theory works incredibly well as a description of our world, he says. “If you just take quantum mechanics as we find it, there doesn’t seem to be any way to read it that doesn’t basically commit you to the wave function representing physical goings-on,” he says.

He would like to see the framework reproduce more complex calculations, such as from quantum field theories that underpin the standard model of particle physics. Historically, this is where non-standard interpretations or reformulations of quantum physics have tended to fail. Barandes says that his framework ought to work for quantum fields, and he plans to extend his work in this direction.

His isn’t a lone, quixotic quest to bring the past back into physics. Cristian Mariani at the University of Italian Switzerland in Lugano works on an unorthodox approach to quantum theory known as spontaneous collapse. It depicts wave function collapse as something that doesn’t happen only when you try to measure things, but can spontaneously occur at any time. Spontaneous collapse models produce predictions that are distinct from those of standard quantum theory, but no experiment has yet provided enough reason to reject standard quantum mechanics in favour of spontaneous collapse. But if quantum laws are amended in a non-Markovian way, allowing spontaneous collapse models to become history-laden, then new experimental tests open up, says Mariani.

Questioning the role of Markovianity in quantum physics is important in itself, he says. “In physics, and in philosophy of physics, this was the kind of assumption that we made without explicitly defending it.” In part, that’s because of the mathematical complexities of non-Markovian theories, and the enduring appeal to philosophers of Occam’s razor, the idea that the simplest solutions are the best. Grappling with the assumption might lead researchers to rethink the nature of physical laws themselves, says Mariani.

It isn’t just our understanding of quantum theory that could be sharpened up, either; so could our conceptions of time and the significance of the present moment. Until the 20th century, philosophers had long argued that the present moment is privileged. In the sense that the past has ceased to be and the future is yet to exist, you might indeed argue that only the present can claim to be truly real. This point of view is known as presentism, and it depicts us as observers living on a wavefront of “now”, ploughing from the past into the future.

Physicists are unclear about the true meaning of now Getty Images

Einstein’s space- and time-warping theories of relativity seemed to put paid to that privileging of the present. Within relativity, it is impossible to get all observers to even agree on a single, simultaneous “now”. The alternative view, which Einstein’s relativity is more friendly towards, is called eternalism. It states that all of the past, present and future exist simultaneously. We exist at a fixed point in this block of space and time, and the flow of time past us is essentially an illusion.

Since the advent of Einstein’s relativity, “most people think that presentism is always on the defensive”, says philosopher David Builes at Princeton University. In 2025, he and his Princeton colleague Michele Odisseas Impagnatiello went on the offensive, arguing that presentism is backed by centuries of experiments whose outcomes haven’t deviated from predictions of Markovian laws of physics that only really require that the present be real. “This isn’t an argument from the armchair; it’s an empirical argument,” says Impagnatiello. Conversely, the pair argue, if a non-Markovian, history-laden interpretation of quantum physics prevails, it will force them to abandon presentism.

We’re a long way off any such proof as yet. “Ideally, we would have a case in which a non-Markovian interpretation is superior in the sense that it makes novel predictions that orthodox quantum mechanics doesn’t make,” says Impagnatiello – a view echoed by Wallace.

Barandes says that one place where his framework may touch the world of experiments is in quantum computing. Quantum computers derive enhanced capabilities through superposition and entanglement effects that, in Barandes’s view, are all really fronts for influences of the past. “A quantum computer is secretly a non-Markovian computer,” he says. “It’s not just the present arrangement of the bits that matters, but also the past arrangements.” There are currently only a few cases where researchers have unambiguously proved that using quantum computers is the only way to solve a particular problem. Thinking about them in a non-Markovian way might lead to the identification of new situations in which they are clear game changers, says Barandes.

Glick agrees there is general value in seeing how far weakening or dropping the Markovian assumption can get us, even if other descriptions of nature never get fully ruled out. “At a certain point, we might find that, well, it’s better to drop that assumption, that then we get a more fruitful result,” he says. “That’s not a direct, empirical kind of confirmation or disconfirmation, but this is how science often works.”

Taking the past seriously touches the foundations of physics in a sweeping and profound way, and that makes it worth pursuing, says Barandes. “I think that this framework may have something to tell us about the way the world really is,” he says. “As a philosopher, I care about that.” It’s certainly food for thought as I prepare my morning smoothie.

articles.personality_title: New theory in quantum physics suggests the past shapes the present and future
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Quantum physics is famous for strange ideas, like particles being in many states at once. One example is Schrödinger’s cat, a thought experiment where a cat is both alive and dead until we check. Scientists have long wondered why quantum physics behaves this way and what it means for the nature of time.

**What happened** – A researcher named Jacob Barandes proposed a new idea: the weird effects in quantum physics happen because the past influences the present more than we thought. Instead of ignoring history, his theory includes “ghost” versions of particles that represent past states. This helps explain quantum oddities without needing the cat to be both alive and dead at the same time.

**Impact** – This new view could solve puzzles about how particles stay connected even when far apart, known as quantum entanglement. It also challenges the usual idea that only the present matters for predicting the future. If the past really matters, it might change how we understand time itself. The theory could help improve quantum computers by showing how past states affect their power.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to test if this idea can predict new results that standard quantum physics cannot. Researchers also plan to apply the theory to more complex physics, like particle fields. If experiments support this view, it might shift how we think about time and the universe.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new quantum theory suggests that the past plays a crucial role in shaping the present and future, offering fresh insight into time and quantum mysteries.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle théorie quantique suggère que le passé façonne le présent et le futur
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La physique quantique est connue pour ses idées étranges, comme les particules pouvant être dans plusieurs états à la fois. Un exemple célèbre est le chat de Schrödinger, où un chat est à la fois vivant et mort jusqu’à ce qu’on regarde. Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps pourquoi la physique quantique fonctionne ainsi et ce que cela signifie pour la nature du temps.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un chercheur nommé Jacob Barandes a proposé une nouvelle idée : les effets bizarres en physique quantique viennent du fait que le passé influence le présent plus qu’on ne le pensait. Au lieu d’ignorer l’histoire, sa théorie inclut des versions « fantômes » des particules qui représentent des états passés. Cela aide à expliquer les étrangetés quantiques sans que le chat soit à la fois vivant et mort.

**Impact** – Cette nouvelle vision pourrait résoudre des énigmes sur la façon dont les particules restent reliées même éloignées, ce qu’on appelle l’intrication quantique. Elle remet aussi en question l’idée que seul le présent compte pour prédire l’avenir. Si le passé compte vraiment, cela pourrait changer notre compréhension du temps. La théorie pourrait aussi améliorer les ordinateurs quantiques en montrant comment les états passés influencent leur puissance.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques veulent tester si cette idée peut prédire de nouveaux résultats que la physique quantique standard ne peut pas. Ils prévoient aussi d’appliquer la théorie à des domaines plus complexes, comme les champs de particules. Si les expériences confirment cette idée, cela pourrait changer notre façon de penser le temps et l’univers.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle théorie quantique suggère que le passé joue un rôle crucial pour façonner le présent et le futur, offrant un nouvel éclairage sur le temps et les mystères quantiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva teoría cuántica sugiere que el pasado moldea el presente y el futuro
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La física cuántica es famosa por ideas extrañas, como que las partículas pueden estar en muchos estados a la vez. Un ejemplo es el gato de Schrödinger, un experimento mental donde un gato está vivo y muerto hasta que se observa. Los científicos han preguntado por qué la física cuántica se comporta así y qué significa para la naturaleza del tiempo.

**Qué pasó** – Un investigador llamado Jacob Barandes propuso una idea nueva: los efectos extraños en la física cuántica ocurren porque el pasado influye en el presente más de lo que se pensaba. En lugar de ignorar la historia, su teoría incluye versiones “fantasma” de partículas que representan estados pasados. Esto ayuda a explicar las rarezas cuánticas sin que el gato esté vivo y muerto a la vez.

**Impacto** – Esta nueva visión podría resolver misterios sobre cómo las partículas se mantienen conectadas aunque estén lejos, llamado entrelazamiento cuántico. También cuestiona la idea de que solo el presente importa para predecir el futuro. Si el pasado realmente importa, podría cambiar cómo entendemos el tiempo. La teoría podría ayudar a mejorar las computadoras cuánticas mostrando cómo los estados pasados afectan su poder.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren probar si esta idea puede predecir resultados nuevos que la física cuántica estándar no puede. También planean aplicar la teoría a física más compleja, como los campos de partículas. Si los experimentos apoyan esta idea, podría cambiar cómo pensamos el tiempo y el universo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una nueva teoría cuántica sugiere que el pasado juega un papel clave para formar el presente y futuro, ofreciendo una nueva visión sobre el tiempo y los misterios cuánticos.

articles.title: The public trusts scientists with AI — more than it does anyone else
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03578-yPublic confidence in scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence remains high, but that trust comes with conditions.
articles.content:
Almost half of survey respondents across nine countries thought that scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence would make society better. Credit: gorodenkoff/iStock via Getty

Scientists are perceived as the group of people most likely to have a positive impact on society through their use of generative artificial intelligence, finds a survey published by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism in Oxford, UK, on 29 October1.

The survey, of nearly 19,000 people across nine countries, found that 46% of respondents think that AI use by scientists will make society better.

People who use AI tools on a daily or weekly basis were also overwhelmingly found to trust more strongly in the positive impact of the technology across all sectors than were those who seldom or never use it.

AI scientists are changing research — institutions, funders and publishers must respond

In 2024 and 2025, the team surveyed six countries, selected to provide cross-national variety among high- and upper-middle-income countries with broadly comparable levels of digital-media use. They were Japan, Argentina, France, Denmark, the United States and the United Kingdom. In 2026, Australia, Finland and Norway were added. Information was collected from about 2,000 people from each country.

Among the questions survey participants were asked was how much better or worse they thought each of ten groups’ use of generative AI would make their life or society. These groups included the government, politicians and political parties and ordinary people.

Scientists ranked top in terms of public trust, closely followed by health-care professionals. By contrast, politicians and political parties were perceived as having the worst impact through their AI use (see ‘With great power’).

The results did not surprise Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, co-author of the report and a communication researcher at the University of Copenhagen: scientists and health-care professionals performed well in the team’s 2025 survey, too2. As part of that investigation, respondents were asked whether generative AI would improve or worsen their experience of interacting with various sectors. Then, scientists ranked second of 12, behind only search-engine companies.

This year, the team explored why certain groups were and were not trusted by assessing different sectors’ perceived ability, benevolence and integrity in their use of AI. “Much of the public believe that scientists are able to use generative AI well, are relatively benevolent in their use of it and have relatively high integrity,” says Nielsen.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant positive public perception and trust in scientists' use of generative AI, highlighting broad societal optimism about AI's beneficial impact when guided by trusted experts. This reflects meaningful societal attitudes towards technology with potential large-scale benefits and calls for responsible institutional responses.
articles.personality_title: Scientists earn highest public trust in using AI for society’s benefit
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A recent survey looked at how people in nine countries feel about different groups using generative artificial intelligence (AI). Generative AI is a type of technology that can create content like text, images, or music.

**What happened** – Nearly 19,000 people were asked whether they think AI use by groups like scientists, politicians, or healthcare workers would make life better or worse. The survey found that 46% of people believe scientists’ use of AI will improve society. Scientists were trusted more than any other group, including healthcare professionals, politicians, and the government.

**Impact** – This shows that many people believe scientists can use AI responsibly and for good reasons. They think scientists have the skills, kindness, and honesty needed to handle AI well. On the other hand, politicians and political parties were seen as the least trustworthy in using AI. People who use AI regularly also tend to trust its benefits more.

**What's next step** – Because scientists are trusted to use AI wisely, research institutions, funders, and publishers may need to support and guide how AI is used in science. This could help AI bring more positive changes in medicine, technology, and other areas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Most people trust scientists more than anyone else to use AI in ways that help society and improve our lives.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques bénéficient de la plus grande confiance du public pour l’utilisation de l’IA au profit de la société
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Une récente enquête a examiné l’opinion des habitants de neuf pays sur l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle générative (IA) par différents groupes. L’IA générative est une technologie capable de créer du contenu comme du texte, des images ou de la musique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Près de 19 000 personnes ont été interrogées pour savoir si elles pensaient que l’utilisation de l’IA par des groupes comme les scientifiques, les politiciens ou les professionnels de santé améliorerait ou détériorerait la vie. L’enquête a révélé que 46 % des personnes croient que l’utilisation de l’IA par les scientifiques améliorera la société. Les scientifiques étaient plus dignes de confiance que tout autre groupe, y compris les professionnels de santé, les politiciens et le gouvernement.

**Impact** – Cela montre que beaucoup de gens pensent que les scientifiques peuvent utiliser l’IA de manière responsable et pour de bonnes raisons. Ils estiment que les scientifiques ont les compétences, la bienveillance et l’honnêteté nécessaires pour bien gérer l’IA. En revanche, les politiciens et les partis politiques étaient considérés comme les moins dignes de confiance dans l’utilisation de l’IA. Les personnes qui utilisent régulièrement l’IA ont aussi tendance à en faire davantage confiance.

**Étape suivante** – Puisque les scientifiques sont considérés comme fiables pour utiliser l’IA à bon escient, les institutions de recherche, les financeurs et les éditeurs pourraient devoir soutenir et guider l’utilisation de l’IA en science. Cela pourrait aider l’IA à apporter plus de changements positifs dans la médecine, la technologie et d’autres domaines.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – La plupart des gens font davantage confiance aux scientifiques qu’à quiconque pour utiliser l’IA de manière à aider la société et améliorer nos vies.
articles.personality_title_es: Los científicos ganan la mayor confianza pública en el uso de la IA para el beneficio de la sociedad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Una encuesta reciente analizó cómo se sienten las personas en nueve países sobre el uso de la inteligencia artificial generativa (IA) por diferentes grupos. La IA generativa es una tecnología que puede crear contenido como texto, imágenes o música.

**Qué pasó** – Casi 19,000 personas respondieron si creen que el uso de IA por grupos como científicos, políticos o profesionales de la salud mejoraría o empeoraría la vida. La encuesta encontró que el 46% de las personas piensa que el uso de IA por parte de los científicos mejorará la sociedad. Los científicos fueron los más confiables, seguidos por profesionales de la salud, mientras que políticos y partidos políticos fueron los menos confiables.

**Impacto** – Esto muestra que muchas personas creen que los científicos pueden usar la IA de manera responsable y con buenas intenciones. Piensan que los científicos tienen las habilidades, la bondad y la honestidad necesarias para manejar bien la IA. Además, quienes usan IA con regularidad tienden a confiar más en sus beneficios.

**Próximo paso** – Dado que los científicos son confiables para usar la IA sabiamente, las instituciones de investigación, financiadores y editoriales podrían necesitar apoyar y guiar el uso de la IA en la ciencia. Esto podría ayudar a que la IA traiga cambios positivos en medicina, tecnología y otros campos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La mayoría de las personas confían más en los científicos que en cualquier otro grupo para usar la IA de forma que beneficie a la sociedad y mejore nuestras vidas.
